question:
A 43-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of nausea and one episode of vomiting over
the past day. He denies any triggering factors except for a headache yesterday, for which he took
acetaminophen. The headache was bilateral, dull, and rated 8/10 in severity. He states he has never
experienced similar symptoms before. His medical history includes hypertension, biliary colic, and a
prior hospitalization for delirium tremens after attempting to abruptly stop alcohol use. When
questioned about his alcohol consumption, he hesitantly mentions “just a couple of drinks here and
there.” He reports mild right upper abdominal pain that started this morning but denies changes in
vision, bowel habits, fever, or weight loss. On physical exam, tenderness is noted in the right upper
quadrant, but it does not worsen with inhalation. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s
symptoms? Answer Choices: (A) Obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstone (B) Hepatic abscess
formation due to bacterial infection (C) Acute pancreatitis due to alcohol use (D) Accumulation of
N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine in the liver (E) Acute viral hepatitis due to underlying risk factors (F)
Upregulation of alpha-2 adrenergic receptors (G) Alcoholic ketoacidosis due to prolonged alcohol
consumption (H) Acute alcoholic hepatitis due to recent binge drinking (I) Hepatotoxicity from chronic
acetaminophen use (J) Drug-induced cholestasis from acetaminophen overdose
 A. Hepatic abscess formation due to bacterial infection
B. Hepatotoxicity from chronic acetaminophen use
C. Acute viral hepatitis due to underlying risk factors
D. Upregulation of alpha-2 adrenergic receptors
E. Obstruction of the cystic duct by gallstone
F. Drug-induced cholestasis from acetaminophen overdose
G. Alcoholic ketoacidosis due to prolonged alcohol consumption
H. Acute pancreatitis due to alcohol use
I. Acute alcoholic hepatitis due to recent binge drinking
J. Accumulation of N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine in the liver
